2. The relevant facts, in short, are that the present pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 Md. Redoyanul Islam as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1996 in the Court of the learned Senior-Assistant Judge, Modhukhali, Faridpur against the pre-emptee-petitioners and opposite party Nos. 2-17 for pre-emption of the case land measuring 42 decimals as described in the schedule of pre-emption application under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 contending, inter-alia, that the pre-emptor-opposite party No.1 is a co-sharer tenant in the case jote by way of purchase and his co-sharer vendor-opposite party No. 2, Most. Tahera Khatun sold 42 decimals of land to the pre-emptee-petitioner Nos.l-2 by a registered sale deed dated 16.09.1996 beyond-the knowledge of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptee-opposite party No. 2 also did not serve any statutory notice of transfer upon the pre-emptor and the other co-sharers of the case jote. It has been further alleged that the pre-emptee-petitioners are not the co-sharer tenants to the case land but a stranger purchaser and having learnt about the disputed transfer he took out the certified copy of the said deed of transfer dated 16.09.1996 and thereafter filed the case within time for pre-emption of the case land on depositing the statutory amount of money. 

 Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy the learned Advocate submits that the Courts below seriously erred in law in allowing pre-emption without properly considering the evidence on record and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the application for pre-emption is not maintainable in law inasmuch as sonic of the S.A. recorded tenants namely Malekunnesa and Rezia Khatun have not been impleaded in the pre-emption application as parties which is mandatory in Section 96 of the State. Acquisition and Tenancy Act He further subinits that section 6 of the Land Reform Ordinance. 1984 debars eviction from the homestead and thus the case land being also homestead, the petitioners who are in possession of the homestead, cannot be evicted from the homestead Lastly Mr. Goutam Kumar Roy submits that the case is also barred by limitation but both the courts below brushing-aside all these vital aspect of the case mechanically allowed the pre-emption in favour of the pre-emptor -opposite party No.1 which cannot be sustained in law and as such the impugned judgment and order dated 27.03.2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Faridpur is liable to be set aside. 

 8. I have gone through the judgments of the Courts below and also had the opportunity of examining the entire evidence of P. W. an O.P.Ws 1-2. It appears that the deed of transfer was registered on 16.09.1996 and the application for pre-emption having been filed on 30.11.1996 i.e. within the statuary period of limitation, provided in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 and the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court upon consideration of the evidence on record having rightly held that the Case was not barred by limitation. It also appears from the findings of the Courts below that there was no defect of parties inasmuch as there was no specific objection with regard to defect the parties by giving necessary particulars of the remaining co-sharer tenants in the disputed khatian at the earliest opportunity. On this point the finding of the learned Senior Assistant Judge is quoted below:- 

 This view clearly shows that the learned Munsif misconceived as to what is meant by the expression "co-sherer in the holding". When Nurul Islam was a co-sharer in one of the plots of khatian he was certainly a co-sharer in the holding. But failure of the pre-emptors to implead him in the application for pre-emption is a serious defect of party since impleading of a co-sharer, whether by inheritance or by purchase, is a mandatory provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The application for pre-emption is therefore liable to be dismissed, as has been rightly held by the appellate Court. This omission was pointed out at the earliest point of time but the omission was not supplied. In the circumstances, the impugned order of the High Court Division restoring the trial Court's order allowing pre-emption is not sustainable in law. 

 12. Be that as it may, the intention of the legislature according to provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is very clear that to shut the door against all strangers, who shall encroach upon the ownership and possession of the real co-sharers and whereupon the real co-sharers can remain in enjoyment of their property and others cannot interfere with their right and possession. In the instant case admittedly the pre-emptee-petitioners are strangers to the case land and they could not substantiate their case by adducing reliable evidence to show that the pre-emptor's claim of pre-emption is barred by any law or the pre-emptor was not entitled under the law to get an order of pre-emption in his favour. So, 1 find substance and force in the submission of the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor opposite party that both the Courts below upon considering the evidences on record and the attending facts and circumstances of the case rightly held that the Pre-emptee petitioners have miserably failed to prove that the case is bad for defect of parties or otherwise the pre-emption case suffers form any legal infirmity by any evidence either documentary or ocular.
